classification.difficultyReason: Requires locating quarter and three-quarter cumulative positions, reading two estimates from the supplied ogive and subtracting. Evaluating Oscar's claim requires distinguishing six observations in a class interval from six observations at its centre.

content.prompt:
A retailer has collected data on the number of televisions that he sold each week in 2012.

He grouped the data into classes and displayed the data using a cumulative frequency histogram and polygon (ogive).

spec.description: Unfilled cumulative frequency histogram and polygon with the source title, axis wording, labelled scales and graph-reading grid. Title uses house sentence case.
spec.answerVisibility: All graph data are permanent student givens; no quartile readings or answer guides are included.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use the cumulative frequency polygon to determine the interquartile range.

answer.worked:
Total frequency is $52$.

$\begin{aligned}\text{Position of }Q_1&=0.25\times52=13\\\text{Position of }Q_3&=0.75\times52=39\end{aligned}$

Read across from cumulative frequencies $13$ and $39$ to the polygon, then down to the horizontal axis:

$Q_1\approx190$ televisions and $Q_3\approx470$ televisions.

$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{IQR}&=Q_3-Q_1\\&\approx470-190\\&=280\text{ televisions}\end{aligned}$

inlines.text: Oscar said that the retailer sold 300 televisions in 6 of the weeks in 2012. Is he correct?
Give a reason for your answer.

answer.short: No. The six weeks belong to the class between 250 and 350 televisions; the grouped data do not show exactly 300 televisions.
answer.worked: $28-22=6$ weeks belong to the class between $250$ and $350$ televisions. The individual weekly sales have been lost through grouping, so Oscar cannot conclude that exactly $300$ televisions were sold in each of those weeks.
